Avery Coleman

gap-007 · supplement · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I like noticing things. I do not always know what they mean. People sometimes hear one fact and act like I am the bug expert, which is uncomfortable when I cannot identify the very bug they found. I also do normal boring phone stuff. I do not spend every evening in the dirt. I think I want more biology, but I want to find out what the harder class actually feels like.

  • family: Lives with their parents and older brother; grandparents nearby host frequent Sunday lunches.
  • finances: Comfortable finances and stable housing; family can usually afford chosen supplies.
  • geography: Denton, Texas; spends several weeks each summer with relatives near Tyler.
  • cultureLanguages: English-speaking household; family accepts their pronouns, while a few distant relatives remain inconsistent.
  • school: Public high school; uses hearing aids and has agreed classroom accommodations.
  • accessOpportunities: Home internet, a small yard, public nature programs, library materials, and accessible seating arranged through school.
  • Age 4–5

    At four Avery loved watering the patch of dirt beneath a tree and searching for moving things afterward. They did not distinguish worms from roots at first. Their brother supplied dramatic names for every discovery. Avery also enjoyed indoor blanket forts, especially when rain made the backyard games impossible.

  • Age 6–7

    At six they received hearing aids and complained more about itchy ears than about the classroom changes adults discussed. A teacher offered a better seat and checked instructions privately. Avery kept bringing home leaves and once cried when a carefully saved caterpillar disappeared from an uncovered shoebox overnight.

  • Age 8–9

    At eight they borrowed an insect guide but mostly used the pictures. Their grandfather helped make a ventilated observation container and return small animals outdoors. Avery liked repeated observation and disliked being told to touch everything. They were happy to watch a spider from a distance without proving bravery.

  • Age 10–11

    At ten they kept a notebook of pill bugs found beneath the same stones. The drawings were rough and the dates fairly consistent. A cousin called the hobby boring; Avery agreed it probably looked boring and continued. They also spent hours playing cooperative building games with two friends from school.

  • Age 12–13

    At twelve a nature-program leader helped them compare observations without claiming that every difference meant a discovery. Avery had been excited about a pattern that disappeared when they checked again. They felt foolish for a week. The next summer they started another notebook, with fewer dramatic titles on the pages.

  • Age 14–15

    At fourteen they took biology and enjoyed learning how small organisms survive in changing conditions. Group discussions could be tiring when everyone spoke at once; this did not predict which activities they liked. They loved noisy family games when they could follow turns. They disliked babysitting, including the constant need to interpret someone else’s crying.

  • Age 16

    Now sixteen Avery checks a shaded yard corner after rain and joins nature walks when transport works. They can describe familiar organisms carefully but are unsure about identification beyond their guide. Friends encourage them to post videos; they prefer keeping notes private. Their current ambition is to take a more demanding biology class without dropping their game nights.

Life now

  • enjoys: Repeated outdoor observation · Cooperative building games · Biology explanations
  • avoids: Pressure to handle every animal · Babysitting · Posting personal videos
  • activities: Rainfall and yard notes · Occasional nature walks · Weekly online games with friends
  • demonstratedSkills: Records dates consistently · Describes visible differences carefully · Revises a claim after checking
  • unfamiliarActivities: Microscope work beyond school lessons · Animal treatment · Extended field trips away from family
  • motivations: Understanding small changes · Having a private interest that is still taken seriously
  • ambitions: Take a more demanding biology class · Keep enough free time for friends
  • struggles: Embarrassment after incorrect identifications · Listening fatigue in overlapping discussion · Pressure to turn hobbies into content
  • supports: Supportive family · Nature-program leader · School accommodations
  • practicalConstraints: Transport to walks · Listening fatigue can limit long group sessions · Most advanced equipment only available at school

Still uncertain: Does curiosity persist through more formal laboratory reporting? · What mix of solitary observation and collaborative work suits them?
